questions.question: What does `T` mean in `public class Box<T> { public T Value; }`?
options: A specific built-in type called T
A type parameter — a placeholder filled in with a real type when the class is used
It means the class only works with strings
A typo — it should be a real type name
questions.explanation: `T` is a placeholder. `Box<int>` and `Box<string>` are both valid, independent uses of the same class definition, with `T` replaced by `int` or `string` respectively.

questions.question: What's wrong with this?
options: Compile error — box.Value must be an int, since box is a Box<int>
It compiles but crashes at runtime
Box<int> doesn't have a Value property
questions.explanation: Once `T` is fixed to `int` for this particular `Box<int>`, `Value` is strictly an `int` property. Generics are still fully type-checked by the compiler — that's the whole benefit over using `object` for everything.

questions.question: Why does `Max<T>(T a, T b)` need `where T : IComparable<T>`?
questions.code: public static T Max<T>(T a, T b) => a.CompareTo(b) > 0 ? a : b;
options: It doesn't need it, this compiles as-is
Without the constraint, the compiler doesn't know T has a CompareTo method — the constraint requires T to implement IComparable<T>, which guarantees CompareTo exists
Constraints are required on every generic method
IComparable<T> makes the method run faster
questions.explanation: Without a constraint, the compiler only knows `T` could be ANY type, so it can't assume `.CompareTo()` exists. The `where` clause promises 'T will always implement IComparable<T>', which unlocks calling `.CompareTo()` in the body.

questions.question: What prints?
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO — Last In, First Out. Push order was 1,2,3; Pop returns the most recently pushed first: 3, then 2.

questions.question: What does `default(T)` evaluate to when `T` is `bool`? When `T` is `string`?
questions.explanation: `default` gives each type's zero-value: value types get their natural zero (`false` for bool, `0` for int), reference types (like `string`) get `null`.

questions.question: `Pair<TFirst, TSecond>` can have `TFirst` and `TSecond` be the same actual type when used, e.g. `Pair<int, int>`.
questions.explanation: Type parameters are independent placeholders — nothing stops you from substituting the same real type for both when you use the generic class.
